title: Pauri 24, sound: ant na siftee
hookLine: ant na siftee kahan na ant
tomorrow: Pauri 24, meaning: no end to praise

lines: NO END, NO END, NO END.
cards: Yesterday's hero was an ant. Today, the first word of Pauri 24 is ant too, spelled the same in English letters. In Punjabi, though, ant means end: the finish, the limit, the last page.
And this stanza uses that word again and again, only to say there isn't one. No end, no end, no end. It's as if the whole stanza is a song about a road with no last mile.
Today, just its first line, and the sound of it.

teach.b: The first line, in the original: ant na siftee kahan na ant. Word by word. Ant, with a short a, UNT: end, limit.

Siftee, SIF-tee: praises, qualities. It comes from sifat, an Arabic word that traveled through Persian, meaning an attribute, a quality worthy of praise; Sikhs speak of sifat salaah, praise and glory.
Kahan: saying, telling. So: no end to the praises, and no end to the telling of them. Now the shape.
The line starts with ant and ends with ant.

teach.h: ANT AT BOTH ENDS OF THE LINE.
teach.b: The word for end sits at both ends, like two bookends, and between them the line says there's no end. The shape plays against the meaning; that's poetry working before the meaning arrives.
The rest of the stanza keeps going, in paraphrase: no end to His works, no end to His giving, no end to seeing, no end to hearing. Line after line, ant, and na.

Guru Nanak is generally described as writing in the everyday speech of his region rather than a classical language, and his words draw on many sources: Punjabi, words from Sanskrit, words from Persian and Arabic, like sifat here.
Tomorrow, what the whole stanza means. Today, the sound: end at both ends, and no end in the middle.

how: Pauri 24 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; its repeated word ant, end, gives the stanza a steady, rolling rhythm that many Sikhs know by heart.

games.why: ant na siftee kahan na ant: ant at the start, ant at the finish, and between them, no end.

practice: Say the line aloud, ant na siftee, kahan na ant, and feel it start and finish on the same word; say it twice more, slower. Then sit with the breath: each one ends and another begins, and there's no last one you can feel coming.
Rest in that rolling, one breath after another.
